modules.name: Back The Way You Came
modules.author: CC0
modules.description: An endless liminal office, generated rather than modelled. There is no level file and no mesh: every partition, every ceiling tile and every dead fluorescent tube is decided by hashing an integer cell index, so the building is unbounded in all four directions and identical for everyone who runs it. The geometry is a 2D problem wearing a 3D coat - partitions run floor to ceiling without exception, so the whole maze is a plane figure extruded and the scene distance is nothing more than min(floor, ceiling, footprint), where footprint is a 2D box SDF evaluated over the 3x3 cells around the sample. That is why a 128-step march through an infinite building costs about what a single sphere costs: the expensive dimension was never there. One cell holds one partition, with its orientation, length, lateral offset and slide read off a four-component hash of the cell id and a small chance of a square pillar instead; doorways are punched by subtracting a second, shorter box, and because that hole is height-dependent the subtraction is the only place the third dimension enters the maze at all. The camera has to be able to GO somewhere, which a hash alone will not guarantee, so one lane of cells is forced empty - a cell is skipped when its centre lies within about a cell of a smooth wandering curve x = path(z) - and the camera walks that same curve. The corridor is therefore carved by the very function that drives the walk and can never be walled off; turn wander to zero and it straightens into a single long hallway. Light is the whole subject. Troffers sit on their own lattice, 2x4 panels with a quarter of them dead and a few of them dying, and every surface gathers from the nine nearest treating each as a RECTANGLE rather than a point: the closest point on the panel is clamped to its extents, so a wall a metre below a tube gets the long soft falloff a real one does instead of a hotspot. A shadow ray is fired only at the strongest of the nine and the other eight are carried by ambient occlusion, which is what keeps a nine-light scene at the cost of a one-light scene. A second, coarse march then accumulates in-scattering from those same panels into the fog, and that is what puts the hazy halo around every fixture and the shafts down the far end of the corridor - the glow is integrated along the ray rather than smeared on afterwards, so it sits correctly in front of and behind the geometry. The surfaces are procedural too: wallpaper as a half-drop repeat of one of four motifs (a chevron stack, a damask lily, a sparse dot and a striped bead), drop-ceiling tile as a two-octave stipple with water rings, discoloured panels and the occasional missing one, and carpet as two octaves of value noise at loop-pile frequency with traffic wear and damp. None of that survives contact with a horizon unless something stands in for a mip chain, and fading by DISTANCE alone is not enough - a wall seen edge-on packs a hundred tiles into ten pixels while still an arm's length away. So each surface is told how many metres of itself one pixel covers, which is the pixel's world size at the hit distance divided by the grazing cosine, and each texture fades toward its own average as that footprint approaches its feature size. Without the cosine term the chevrons alias into broad moire arcs across every oblique wall; with it they simply go quiet. The same care is why the shadow ray is aimed along the WEIGHTED MEAN of the nine panel directions rather than at the strongest of them: the strongest one changes as you slide along a wall, the loci where two panels tie are smooth curves, and the shadow term steps across them - which paints the wall in concentric arcs. A mean moves continuously and has no seams. Then it is put on tape: the ray direction is bent by a barrel term and shoved sideways per scanline BEFORE it is ever traced, so the tracking error lives in the optics rather than being painted over them, and the frame picks up scanlines, head-switching hash along the bottom edge, dropouts, grain, edge tint and a lifted black. Where the lights have failed is decided by a slowly varying field over the plan rather than one tube at a time, so the dead ones clump: a flat per-panel probability scatters them evenly and every distance ends up equally lit, whereas clumping puts a genuinely dark room at the end of a corridor. That same field dims the ambient and the fog, so a dark zone is dark the whole way through instead of merely missing its highlights. The troffers land in the tile grid rather than across it: the tile size is a quarter of the light spacing, so a panel centred at (lid + 0.5)*LG sits on an exact multiple of the tile - a T-bar - and every fixture straddles a grid line by half a tile until x is offset by half a tile and the panel's size is taken from the spacing instead of from fixed metres, which keeps it exactly one tile by two at any setting. And sometimes there is a figure standing down the corridor - pale, featureless, its legs dissolving before they reach the floor, built to real proportions out of ten pieces with an egg-shaped head, a short neck, sloped shoulders, a chest narrowing to a waist, arms with an elbow and legs with a knee. A neck is a width pinch rather than a gap, and a capsule ending at the shoulders puts a hemispherical cap a full radius ABOVE its endpoint, so a chest of radius 0.15 ending at 1.50 bulges to the underside of the head and swallows the neck whole; stopping the chest lower and giving the shoulders their own sloped piece takes the silhouette from 0.43 m wide at the shoulders to 0.10 m at the neck to 0.18 m at the head inside twenty centimetres, and that contrast is the neck. A torso is also not round - a circular capsule as wide as a chest is equally deep and reads as a barrel, so z is squashed by 1.45 before the trunk is evaluated. Both of those lean on the same freedom: the tapered capsule is not a valid distance field wherever its radii differ, and the squash breaks the metric outright, and neither matters because the field is only ever sampled. It is never marched as a surface; the distance field does not know about it. It is integrated as a soft volume along the primary ray inside its own bounding sphere - which is also what makes it cheap to break: the sample position can simply be warped before the figure is evaluated, so horizontal slices tear sideways, a slow boil runs underneath, a scanline sweeps down it and the whole thing drops out for the odd beat, all of it updating on an 11 Hz beat rather than continuously, because a value that holds for ninety milliseconds and then jumps reads as a recording fault where a smooth wobble would only read as motion; a second, x-offset density accumulated in the same loop drives the blue channel, giving a real spatial separation rather than a coloured fringe - which is the whole difference between something you can see through and a white statue, and it costs eighteen samples over a few per cent of the frame. The walls occlude it for nothing, because the integration simply stops at whatever the marcher already hit. Rather more than half of the doorway openings are still hung with a leaf, which is a second thin box in the same footprint as the opening - one more box and no extra hash, since fract(g.z*13.7) is decorrelated enough from the g.z that already decided whether there is an opening at all. Thirty-six controls: walk speed, focal length, yaw and pitch, how much the corridor wanders and how sharply it turns, handheld sway, cell size, wall density, doorway frequency, ceiling height, light spacing, what fraction of the tubes still work, brightness, flicker, how much the outages clump into dark zones, haze, fog, a palette that crossfades classic yellow into sickly green, institutional grey and sepia dusk, the wallpaper motif and its scale, baseboard, grime, damp, blood, carpet pile, ambient occlusion, shadow, the figure, how many of them and how badly they glitch, and five tape controls for the analogue damage.

modules.name: Mesmer
modules.author: CC0
modules.description: A black-and-white op-art engine built to be stared at. Everything is computed in log-polar space, where a straight line becomes a logarithmic spiral and simply scrolling the radius is an endless zoom with no seam to repeat. Four harmonics lie over one another - the spiral itself, concentric rings marching outward, radial wedges, and a pair of gratings set a hair out of alignment so they beat against each other into moire - and the sum is squared up into hard black and white. A crossed sine domain warp drags the whole plane around, so the pattern swims rather than merely turning. Every harmonic knows its own screen-space frequency and fades itself toward grey as it approaches one cycle per pixel, which is what keeps the infinite zoom clean instead of boiling into aliasing at the vanishing point. Twenty-four sliders: speed, zoom rate (negative falls inward), spin, radial tightness and arm count, the four layer amounts, warp, breathing, a hardness dial from pure sine to hard square edge, contrast, invert, vignette and grain, plus four more optical effects — Fraser twisted-cord hatching that makes concentric bands read as one continuous spiral, a cafe-wall row offset that sets straight bands leaning, a roving lens that magnifies whatever it wanders over, and a 45-degree halftone dot screen that rebuilds the tone the way it would come off a press. Four more push it further out: a kaleidoscope fold that mirrors the angle into N sectors and turns the spiral into a mandala, self-similar fractal octaves so every band grows bands of its own all the way down, a turbulent fbm warp that makes the plane boil rather than merely sway, and travelling rings of inverted polarity so the whole image keeps turning itself inside out.

modules.name: neptune.exe
modules.author: CC0
modules.description: A Greek paradise pool at the end of the world, seen through a vaporwave haze. A long turquoise pool tiled in a navy grid and ringed with a Greek key border, its water rippling and throwing caustics on the floor, stretches toward a white marble temple: fluted columns, a heavy entablature and a pediment, a neon glow spilling from its doorway. Domed pavilions stand to either side, marble busts watch from their pedestals, balustrades run along the edges and palm trees lean over the water. The whole terrace floats above an endless magenta grid. Behind it all, a huge striped retro sun sinks into wireframe mountains under a purple-pink sky, and every bit of it is mirrored in the pool. SPEED is the camera drift, SUN HEIGHT and SUN SIZE place the sun, STRIPES cuts its bands, WAVES and CAUSTICS stir the water, NEON the glow of the grid and doorway, GRID, MOUNTAINS, PALMS and STATUES switch the set dressing, SCANLINES the CRT look, HUE spins the palette, EXPOSURE the overall light.

modules.name: Not Responding
modules.author: CC0
modules.description: The Windows XP window-trail glitch, rendered with the gloss the era actually wanted. A dialog is being dragged across a Bliss-green hill, and the desktop never repaints behind it, so every position it has ever occupied stays painted on the screen. The trail is not decoration: each copy in the cascade is the SAME window sampled at a point in its own past, drawn oldest first, so what you are looking at is literally the path it has been dragged along. Some stale copies never finished repainting and smear one scanline sideways across their own body. Over the top of that is the Frutiger Aero treatment the period was reaching for and the hardware could not quite manage - Luna titlebars with a specular sweep riding across them, soap bubbles with iridescent films, a sun with lens ghosts, oversaturated skies, bloom, a taskbar with task buttons and a system tray, desktop icons, and a start menu. Everything is drawn from signed distance fields; there is no texture anywhere. Twenty-two sliders and one switch: speed, how many copies survive, the gap between them, drag distance, per-copy glitch jitter, tearing, how much the oldest copies wash out, Aero glass, bubbles, sun flare, cloud cover, vividness, bloom, taskbar, scanlines, vignette, plus how many windows are being dragged at once, desktop icons, the two-pane Luna start menu, open or shut, and the pointer that is still holding the live window's titlebar, and three that decide what the failed repaint left behind - text returning as characters from no alphabet, query dialogs and stray question marks, and rows that tear sideways or invert into a stale selection block.

modules.name: Plexus
modules.author: CC0
modules.description: An endless biomechanical spine - ten of them - coiled around one another and travelling away from you forever. Stacked ribbed plates threaded onto a corrugated cord, a pair of back-swept spikes down each flank, and bundles of flexible conduit running the whole length. Three things make it affordable as a single-pass raymarcher. Z IS THE PARAMETER: each strand is a curve written as a function of the world z, so for any point the nearest piece of that strand is the piece at the point's own z, with no search along the curve and no table. The cross-section then comes out sheared by the strand's slope instead of perpendicular to it, which at this pitch is about a tenth and reads as the plate leaning into the coil; and what falls out is not a distance but an over-estimate by at most sqrt(1 + slope^2), so every strand divides its own field by its own slope bound. That bound has three terms and the one that is easy to miss is the third: the local frame TURNS with z as well as translating, so a point sitting at the plate rim feels another rim-radius times dphi/dz of speed. ONLY THE PLATE REPEATS, AND IT SITS IN THE MIDDLE OF ITS CELL: mod() repetition over-estimates near a cell boundary because the nearest surface may be the neighbour's, so the cord, the dorsal cord and the conduits are all written against z and know nothing about the cell - they run through every wall unbroken, and the field near a wall is therefore small, which is exactly where the over-estimate would otherwise bite. That same rule shapes every surface: ribbing written per cell would break at every joint, since a cell picks up a new roll and a new hash there, while ribbing written against z runs the length of the strand, which is the only way a corrugated tube reads as one. It is paid for in one place - a modulated radius adds amplitude times frequency to the field's slope, so each piece divides by its own bound - and past about five units the ribs are flattened out with distance, because a rib finer than a pixel is noise and, unlike a radius, it cannot be floored: flooring a corrugation only makes a fatter corrugation. AND IT LOOPS: the camera flies at a constant speed and the whole scene is periodic in z, so after one period divided by that speed - fifteen seconds at the defaults - the frame comes back to where it started, measured at a mean difference of 0.31 of one colour step against the frame a period earlier, the residue being float precision in phases that grow with z. Not a crossfade and not a fade to black: every phase is written as k*(n*z + m*zc) with n and m whole, and every per-plate hash is taken on the cell index modulo the number of plates in a period, so advancing the camera by one period maps the scene onto itself. The two controls that would break that, the coil rate and the twist, are integer sliders for the same reason. The braid is two bundles, an inner one coiling one way and an outer one coiling the other, which is what makes them read as intertwined rather than merely parallel; they can never collide because they live in separate radial bands, and within a bundle every strand coils at the same rate, so those cannot collide either. The weaving is a radius that wanders with z, so strands cross over one another in depth without ever touching. A plate is an elliptical footprint - (er - 1) times the smaller semi-axis is a conservative distance to an ellipse - drooping backwards towards a rim that thickens into a heavy bar, with a ladder of ribs across it; the ribs run on the LONG axis because the slope a rib adds is frequency times amplitude over the axis it varies along, so running them that way costs less than half what radial rings did and buys a deeper rib for it. The six conduits round each cord are got for the price of one by folding the angle into a sixth, which is exact because each tube sits in the middle of its own sector and fits inside it; the spikes are mirrored across the strand for the same kind of reason, one primitive drawing a symmetric pair. The plate is deliberately narrow and the SPIKES carry the width, because a bounding volume is a budget: bolting long spikes onto a wide plate pushed the bound out by half, which costs march steps everywhere and forces the two bundles apart until the braid stops being a braid. Light is a key, a headlight, a rim and a translucency term read from the field a little way behind the surface, over a hard narrow highlight on a broad sheen; every colour in the picture sits within a twentieth of one hue, because a complementary glow turns this kind of thing into poster art. There is no sky function at all: the background is black and the fog is a plain multiply into the same black, because at depth the only thing separating one strand from the next is how much of it the fog has eaten, and a lit sky both washes that out and gives the bioluminescence something to compete with. An exponential never reaches zero, though, so on its own it draws a hard edge at the far clip - at any sane density the field is still lit where the march stops, and the braid comes out with a straight cut across it that reads as clipping rather than as distance. Raising the density only moves the edge nearer; the fade needs a factor that is exactly zero at the clip, so the last thing visible is already black by the time the ray runs out of distance to travel; (1-x^2)^2 in x = t/MAXD lands on zero with a zero derivative, so there is no edge there and no knee before it. Each spine also ROLLS about its own axis while its position in the braid stays put, which is what makes them turn on the spot rather than the braid swinging round: the roll is applied to the local frame before the vertebra is built, so plate, spikes, dorsal cord and conduits turn together as one body - spin only the plate and it shears through the conduits welded to it - and it is a rigid rotation, so the distance bound is untouched. It depends only on the clock and the strand index, so it is worked out once a frame into a small global array read back with the loop variable as its index, rather than costing two more transcendentals per strand in every one of the many map calls a pixel makes; and it is in WHOLE turns per period, like the coil rate and the twist, because half a turn at the end of a period would leave every strand at the wrong angle when the camera came back. The bioluminescence runs at a different rate through different parts: one wave whose wavelength and speed are chosen by the material at the hit, so the light crawls along the plates, runs down the cord and races through the conduits, with a golden-angle phase per strand so no two are in step. The glow is gathered with TWO kernels, a tight one for the light on the strand and a faint broad one for the little of it that reaches across the gap - widening a single kernel instead washes the whole frame grey. The broad one is COMPACT rather than exponential, because an exponential is never zero and a ray that misses everything would still gather a little all the way to the far clip, lifting the corners of the frame off black however small its coefficient; a window that vanishes at about one strand spacing means open void accumulates exactly nothing, and the background measures a true zero. Controls: flight speed, coil turns per period, how many strands in each bundle, both radii, the weave, the axis wander and the travelling undulation, the plate twist, the axial spin, dorsal cord, wing span, thickness, plate depth, spikes, ribbing, conduits, per-plate variation, camera distance, swing, focal length and roll, key light, bioluminescence, fog, hue, march steps, antialiasing and exposure.

The glass is an analytic sphere with animated thin-film iridescence, an adjustable index of refraction, and a reflection of the ground in its lower shell. Inside: a churning spiral-armed nebula whose regions burn through a shifting magenta/violet/rose/amber palette with electric cyan wisps, dark absorbing dust lanes, and two layers of tiny 4-pointed stars — with sliders for animation speed, domain warp and turbulence. A fringe of writhing tentacle fingers waves along the orb's rim, magical smoke boils off it, wispy ribbons orbit it, and sixteen alien glyphs drift around it on a spherical orbit, built from ring, spine, track, radial and script families with procedurally generated lettering. Fine atmospheric dust hangs in the air. The terrain carries glowing carved spirals, emissive veins, and its own relief / detail / colour controls. The camera orbits on a slider, and hue rotates independently for orb, ground, effects and the whole frame.

modules.name: REC
modules.author: CC0
modules.description: Running for your life through a black forest at night, first person. The path winds between tall dead trunks that vanish up into fog; a torch bounces in your hand and throws a hard beam through the mist, moonlight leaks through holes in a canopy you never see. Every few seconds you can't help it: you whip round over your shoulder -- and it is still there, a tall gaunt thing loping after you down the path with its arms reaching out, eyes catching the light. Then back to the path. The camera is a body: every footfall jolts it, the hands shake, the torch flickers when you least want it to, and now and then you stumble. SPEED is how fast you run, SHAKE how hard the camera jolts, LOOK BACK how often you check behind you, CLOSENESS how near it has got, TORCH whether you have a light, FLICKER how bad the batteries are, FOG the mist, MOON the moonlight, TREES how thick the forest is, BLUR the smear of a panicked turn, GRAIN the film, EXPOSURE the overall light. It all comes off a worn camcorder tape: VHS sets how chewed up it is -- chroma smeared off the edges, wobbling lines, head-switching noise along the bottom, a tracking band rolling through that tears worst when you look back, dropouts -- and OSD burns in the blinking REC and the running counter.

modules.name: Skrrt
modules.author: CC0. Original. An homage - no marque assets, every number typed in by hand.
modules.description: TRUENO 86 - a 1983 Sprinter Trueno AE86 going down a Japanese mountain pass at night, sideways, on its headlights. The car is one signed distance field built from the real thing's measurements: 4180 long, 1625 wide, 1335 tall on a 2400 wheelbase, 185/60 on fourteens, and the overhangs deliberately unequal - 830 in front, 970 behind - because a body box centred on the axles is what makes a model car look like a toy. The road is a SHEAR OF SPACE: a cross-section drawn once as a polyline - cut face, gutter, six metres of asphalt, shoulder, then nothing - and extruded along z while every sample is displaced sideways and downward by the centreline's own functions, so the whole descending pass is three sines and an exact 2D distance rather than a mesh. Because the profile is a polyline and the road is an extrusion, that distance is EXACT; the shear costs one constant Lipschitz factor and nothing else. The drift is not an animation, it is the road: the car's yaw is the road's heading plus a term proportional to its CURVATURE, so it points into the corner wherever the corner is, the front wheels counter-steer against that angle, the body leans on it, the line runs wide on it and the tyre smoke comes off it. The drift, the camber and the suspension are all one transform on the RAY - the sample is pushed backward through the car's yaw, roll, pitch and a volume-preserving squash before the body is evaluated, and the returned distance is multiplied by the smallest scale factor so the field stays conservative and the march stays legal. Night is what makes it: one dim moon and two headlamps, which are elliptical cones with a flat CUTOFF along the top the way a low beam really is, and they are integrated through the air as well as landed on the road - sixteen taps down the view ray gathering haze, tail-light red and the smoke off the rear tyres, which the tail lights are the only thing lighting because the beams point the other way. The camera is a DIRECTOR rather than a chase rig: every uCut seconds the frame cuts to a shot drawn from a hash of the cut index - front three-quarter, head on, off the bank, chase, down at wheel height, or a roadside pass-by where the camera stops following and the car comes to it - the draw is squared so the front views come up most often, and every shot dollies and swings inside itself, because a cut from one locked-off camera to another is still locked off. Everything on the ground is keyed to the ABSOLUTE distance down the pass rather than to the car, because the car sits at z = 0 forever and anything drawn at its own z is nailed to it - the asphalt, the tar seams every eight metres, the cat's eyes, the guardrail posts and the delineator poles all stream past because of that one substitution, and they carry half a frame of travel of ordered motion blur with them while the car, which is not moving relative to the camera, stays sharp. The reflectors are modelled as RETROREFLECTORS - emission proportional to the beam landing on them, not a specular lobe - which is why they flare white as the pool reaches them and go out the moment it leaves. When the rear quarter leans on the barrier it throws sparks: eighteen ballistic particles shed backward at road speed, each drawn as the segment it swept since the last frame and glowed by the closest distance from the view ray to that segment, with a floor on the radius of what one pixel is worth at that depth - as a density in the volumetric they were invisible, because a spray forty centimetres across is missed by sixteen taps three metres apart. Nothing can clip the mountain: the car's line is clamped by its own SWEPT WIDTH, which for a box yawed by the drift angle is halfW*|cos| + halfL*|sin| - two metres of a six metre road at forty degrees - so the harder it is sideways the less of the road it is allowed to use, and the camera climbs out of the cut face by querying the same cross-section it would otherwise be buried in. Every edge on the car is a hard intersection of planes - no rounded boxes anywhere - because a smoothed corner is a modern renderer's tell. The PS2 look is the render and not a filter: the fragment coordinate is quantised before the ray is built, so the frame is genuinely traced at a couple of hundred lines, then posterised through an ordered 4x4 Bayer dither. Thirty-five controls: body, face, pop-ups, spoiler, paint (as three channels, because a colour input is the one thing hosts disagree about), panda, gloss, wheels, tyre, speed, drift, bumps, lean, curve, grade, camera distance, camera height, camera angle, seconds per cut, lens, headlamps, beam spread, haze, smoke, sparks, motion blur, moon, stars, town, render resolution, colour depth, dither and grain.

modules.name: The Pool Rooms
modules.author: CC0. Plan generation, footprint filtering and the light gather follow the CC0 BACKROOMS shader; the water is original, informed by but not derived from Alexander Alekseev's 'Seascape'.
modules.description: The Poolrooms. An endless tiled natatorium in shallow water, generated rather than modelled: no level file and no mesh, every partition and every arched opening decided by hashing an integer cell index, so the building is unbounded and identical for everyone who runs it. The plan is the backrooms trick - a 2D box SDF over the 3x3 cells around the sample, extruded floor to ceiling, so a 128-step march through an infinite building costs about what a single sphere costs. The openings are what change. A doorway punched with a box is a doorway; an arch has to be a real cross-section, so the opening is built in the plane of the wall as the union of a jamb box and a disc at the springing, then extruded THROUGH the wall - a proper distance field with a bounded gradient, where a semicircular profile written as a height-dependent width would have infinite slope at the crown and tear the march apart there. The water is the subject and it is deliberately NOT marched. Seascape marches its surface because its waves are 0.6 m tall; a pool ripple is 8 mm, which is under a pixel at any distance past arm's length, so the displacement is invisible and only the NORMAL matters: the surface is an analytic plane hit plus one Newton step against the true height, and everything anyone actually sees is in the gradient. The ripple field is four rotated wave trains whose phase is warped by value noise, each moving at a speed proportional to one over the square root of its wavenumber - gravity-wave dispersion - so the long trains outrun the short ones and the field never reads as a single scrolling texture, which is the giveaway in most water. A wake radiates from the camera and decays, so wading disturbs the surface it is wading through. At the far end the ripple cannot be resolved, and it must not simply be faded to a mirror: an unresolved ripple is not a flat surface, it is a rough one, so as the pixel footprint outgrows the wavelength the geometric normal relaxes toward vertical and the specular lobe widens by exactly as much - the shimmer becomes gloss instead of aliasing into sparkle. The surface is then split by Fresnel between a reflection march and a refraction march. The refracted ray carries Beer-Lambert absorption on the way down and picks up the in-scattered pool colour on the way back, which is the whole reason shallow water over white tile is turquoise and deep water is not. Caustics are not a texture: they are the focusing term of the refracted map, computed as one over one plus depth times the Laplacian of the ripple field, so they spread with depth, tighten under a crest, and move with the water rather than under it - and the same field, attenuated by height above the waterline, is what puts the dancing light on the walls and the ceiling, which is the single image everyone has of this place. Every surface is glazed tile, filtered the way the backrooms filters its wallpaper: each point is told how many metres of itself one pixel covers - the pixel's world size at the hit distance divided by the grazing cosine - and the grout is box-filtered against that footprint, decaying to the grid's duty cycle rather than to nothing, because a periodic grid seen edge-on averages to grey and not to white. A course of accent tile runs at the waterline, there is a wet band above it that tracks the live ripple height rather than a fixed level, and the ledges that break the surface are defined relative to the water rather than to the floor, because their entire job is to be half in it. Light is 4 ft square coffers on a lattice snapped to a whole number of ceiling tiles, gathered nine at a time as RECTANGLES with one shadow ray fired along their weighted mean, and a second coarse march accumulates in-scattering into the humid air, which is what puts the shafts down the far end of the hall. Thirty-seven controls: walk, lens, yaw and pitch, corridor wander and turn, sway, cell size, wall density, closed rooms, arch frequency and width, ceiling height, ledge width, water depth, ripple, flow, caustics, clarity, light spacing, working lights, brightness, dark zones, haze, fog, four palettes from chlorine white through warm natatorium, cold blue and sickly green, tile scale, accent course, grime, damp, ambient occlusion, shadow, gloss, and four camcorder controls.
